extra.motion: From the very first frame the woman in the hooded olive parka is already walking straight towards the camera along the muddy grass path, hands deep in her pockets, boots squelching. The camera drifts slowly backwards at her walking pace, keeping her centred and the same size in frame. As she passes the table of mugs and jugs on the right, her eyes flick sideways to it for a moment, then back ahead, face flat and unimpressed. Fine drizzle falls the whole time, beading on her hood. Behind her the stallholders stay at their tables and the man under the umbrella stays seated; the blue gazebo and the open car boots stay where they are. She keeps her mouth closed. Sound: soft steady rain on canvas and parka, wet footsteps, a distant murmur of a crowd. Real, overcast English daylight, handheld-steady.

She starts moving at once: one step forward towards the camera, then another, with the camera easing slowly back in front of her. On the second step she turns her head left to glance at the old computer monitor and teacups under the plastic sheet, gives a tiny, tired breath out through her nose, and looks forward again, still walking. A drop of rain runs off the edge of her hood. The people in the background shift their weight and browse at their own stalls without coming closer. Her expression stays weary and unimpressed; she says nothing. Sound: light rain pattering on the plastic sheeting and gazebo roofs, squelch of mud underfoot, low far-off crowd murmur. Grey natural light, documentary realism.

Locked-off camera, eye level. Immediately the dealer in the flat cap lifts the framed red-brick hospital picture a few centimetres higher towards the camera, beaming, and says cheerfully in a broad English accent: "Hospitals, love. Forty quid." His lips form each word clearly and in time with the voice; he says it once, then holds the grin and gives the frame a small proud tilt. The brown card tag tied with string on the frame keeps its handwritten "NHS £40" exactly as written and stays readable. Drops of rain gather on the front edge of the white gazebo and drip down past the top of the frame. People in the background browse slowly. Sound: his single line, rain dripping off the gazebo, light rain on canvas, a quiet crowd murmur. Natural overcast light.

Static camera. Within the first second the dealer leans in slightly over the box of frames, gives a quick wink, and says brightly in a London-ish English accent: "Hospitals, love. Forty quid." Mouth moves naturally with every syllable, said once and clearly. Then he gives the frame a little waggle as if it's a bargain and keeps smiling at the camera. The hospital photo, the frame and the "NHS £40" tag stay unchanged and legible. Rainwater drips steadily from the gazebo edge; the shoppers behind him stay at a distance under their hoods. Sound: his one line, close and clear, then drips, soft rain, a faint murmur of a crowd. Real-looking, damp grey daylight.

Camera holds still at eye level. Straight away the dealer, holding the framed gavel picture in his left hand, lifts his open right hand and both shoulders in a slow shrug, tilts his head, and says in a dry English accent: "The courts. Slightly used." His mouth matches each word, said once and plainly, with a little half-smile at the end. The card tag hanging from the frame keeps its handwritten "THE COURTS - SLIGHTLY USED" exactly as written. The red-brick picture in the crate in front stays where it is. Light rain falls beyond the white gazebo; people in the background drift slowly between stalls. Sound: his single line, rain on the gazebo roof, a low crowd murmur. Overcast natural light.

Fixed camera. From the first moment the dealer purses his lips, glances down at the gavel picture as if weighing it, then back up to the camera, and with an apologetic shrug of his free hand says, deadpan, in an English accent: "The courts. Slightly used." Lips move clearly and in sync, the line spoken once. He then raises his eyebrows and holds still. The frame, the gavel image and the tag text stay the same and readable. A few raindrops run off the gazebo frame above him; the figures with umbrellas in the background barely move. Sound: his line, gentle rain, a quiet murmur of a crowd. Real, damp English daylight.

Camera stays fixed at standing height. The long black car is already moving in the first second, rolling slowly towards the camera along the rutted mud track, tyres sinking and pushing up brown water from the puddled ruts. It keeps coming, filling more of the frame, then veers slightly and slides past the camera to the left edge, the wet dark bodywork and smooth bonnet staying plain and unadorned. As it passes, the woman with the backpack on the left and the woman holding the teapot turn their heads to follow it; the old man in the flat cap on the right stares after it. Drizzle falls throughout. Sound: a low, quiet engine hum, tyres sucking through mud, splash of puddles, light rain, a crowd murmur that dips. Grey overcast daylight, realistic.

Static, slightly low camera beside the track. Immediately the black car creeps forward at walking pace, mud spraying gently from its front wheels and brown water rippling in the ruts. People at the stalls stop what they are doing: the woman with the backpack steps back half a pace, the woman holding the teapot freezes mid-look, the old man in the flat cap slowly turns his head after it. The car rolls on and passes close by the camera on the left, its dark side gliding through frame, smooth and unadorned, leaving the muddy ruts and the stalls behind it. Rain keeps falling lightly. Sound: soft engine purr, mud and water squelching under heavy tyres, drizzle, a crowd murmur going quiet. Natural, wet daylight.

Camera holds steady. Within the first second the heavy bald man in the pinstripe suit, just out of the open car door, lifts his cane and plants its tip firmly in the mud. The uniformed chauffeur behind him keeps the black umbrella held high over his head. The heavy man then turns his head slowly left, then right, surveying the stalls with a smug, satisfied half-smile, chin up. Meanwhile the thin clerk in glasses hurries forward a few quick steps from the right to stay at his shoulder, clutching the clipboard marked "PURCHASES" to his chest, the word staying readable. Light rain falls; the shoppers behind keep browsing. Nobody speaks. Sound: rain drumming on the umbrella, a squelch as the cane hits mud, quick wet footsteps, distant crowd murmur. Real, overcast daylight.

Static camera. At once the heavy bald man takes one deliberate step forward from the car, the chauffeur moving the umbrella with him to keep him dry, and sets his cane down in the mud with a firm tap. He pauses, looks slowly across the car-boot stalls like a man inspecting property he already owns, and gives a slight smug nod. The thin clerk scurries after him, small hurried steps, head bowed, gripping the "PURCHASES" clipboard, and stops just behind his right shoulder. The car door stays open and the car stays still and plain. Nobody talks. Sound: rain on the umbrella fabric, wet footsteps and mud, a soft murmur of a crowd. Natural grey light, realistic.

Camera locked, close two-shot. From the first moment the heavy bald man, his ringed hand resting on the clerk's shoulder, narrows his eyes and says slowly and smugly in a deep English accent: "All of it." His lips shape the three words clearly, in sync, said once with a pause between "All" and "of it". The clerk beside him, sweat and rain running down his face and fogging his glasses, starts writing faster on the clipboard, pen scratching, eyes darting nervously; his mouth stays closed. The clipboard keeps its printed heading "PURCHASES" readable. The framed pictures and plates on the stall behind stay where they are. Sound: the single line, low and pleased, pen scratching paper, light rain, a faint crowd murmur. Real overcast daylight.

Fixed camera. Immediately the heavy man gives the clerk's shoulder two slow pats, turns his face a little towards him and, savouring it, says in a smooth, posh English voice: "All of it." Mouth moving naturally with each word, said once. The clerk swallows, a bead of sweat sliding down his cheek, and scribbles frantically, the pen racing down the checkboxes on the "PURCHASES" clipboard, which stays legible. Behind them a couple of shoppers browse slowly; the patterned umbrella stays still. Only the heavy man speaks. Sound: his line, the scratch of a hurried pen, gentle rain, soft crowd murmur. Damp grey light, realistic.

Camera completely still. Straight away the woman on the sofa, still in her olive parka, reads her phone, its cool light flickering faintly on her face. Her expression slowly changes from tired to stunned; she slowly lowers the mug of tea in her other hand to her lap and stops moving, just staring at the screen. On the window behind her, raindrops run down the glass in thin trails. The table lamp glows steadily and the candle flame on the coffee table flickers softly. She says nothing; the room is quiet. Sound: rain against the window, a faint tick of the radiator, near silence. Warm lamplight against cold grey window light, real home interior.

Static camera. In the first second her thumb scrolls once on the phone and stops. She reads, blinks, and leans in very slightly towards the screen, the phone's light on her face. The mug in her right hand drifts slowly down towards her knee, forgotten. She holds completely still, mouth slightly open, staring. Water streams down the window panes behind her; the net curtains hang still. The candle flame wavers. Nobody speaks. Sound: steady rain on glass, a soft gust outside, a quiet room. Natural, lamp-lit evening realism.

Camera holds still in the aisle. Right away the thin clerk, standing among the seated bidders, lifts paddle 29 a little higher with a weary sigh, his shoulders sagging, the worn folder tucked under his other arm. The paddle number "29" stays crisp and readable, and the board on the right keeps showing "£150,000" unchanged. A murmur spreads through the marquee; a few seated people turn their heads to look at him. The man at the lectern on the right keeps gesturing silently. The festoon bulbs glow steadily; rain falls lightly on the tent roof. Only the clerk moves much; he does not speak. Sound: a rising murmur of a crowd, rain on canvas, a chair creak. Soft overcast light through the marquee.

Fixed camera. Immediately the clerk pushes paddle 29 up another few inches, arm trembling slightly, and looks towards the lectern with a tired, pleading face. Heads in the rows around him turn; a woman in the back raises her eyebrows. A low murmur rolls through the tent. The "29" on the paddle and the "£150,000" on the board stay exactly as they are and readable. The string lights sway very slightly; the man at the lectern holds his gesture. The clerk keeps his mouth closed. Sound: crowd murmur swelling, light rain on the marquee roof. Natural daylight in a white tent, realistic.

Camera locked, looking up past the seated heads. At once the masked auctioneer, standing behind the wooden lectern, holds his black gloved palm out flat towards the room in a calm, firm "stop", keeping it there for a beat. Then he brings the gavel in his other hand down once on the lectern with a sharp crack, and goes still. His navy balaclava stays exactly the same throughout: the white ring around the face area and the small red triangle over his left eye, fully covering his head, with no opening; only the knitted fabric shows. The blackboard behind keeps its crossed-out figure and "£50" readable. Rain trickles down the clear tent wall behind. Sound: a hush in the crowd, one loud wooden gavel knock, rain on canvas. Soft natural light.

Static camera. Immediately the masked auctioneer slowly raises his gloved left hand a little higher and holds it steady, palm out, unhurried, like a policeman halting traffic. The audience heads in the foreground shift slightly. After a pause he lifts the gavel and strikes the lectern once, firmly, then rests both hands. His head barely moves; the navy balaclava with its white ring and red triangle over his left eye keeps its exact shape and covers him completely, gloves on both hands. The "£50" on the blackboard stays clear and unchanged. Greenery overhead sways faintly; rain streaks the tent window. Sound: the crowd murmur falling quiet, a single crisp gavel knock, gentle rain. Natural overcast light.

Camera holds still. From the first second, more and more of the seated people behind the front row raise their round "£50" paddles, one after another, until the hall is full of them; each paddle reads "£50" clearly. In the front row the heavy bald man in the pinstripe suit twists round in his chair to look back at them, face reddening, mouth set in outrage, then turns his head back towards the lectern. The thin clerk beside him sinks a little lower, holding his paddle in his lap. The masked auctioneer at the right edge stands still with gavel raised, his navy balaclava with white ring and red triangle unchanged. Nobody speaks. Sound: rustle of paddles going up, a rising murmur, light rain on the marquee. Real, soft tent daylight.

Static camera. Immediately a ripple of paddles goes up across the tent: the ordinary people in the rows behind lift their "£50" paddles, a few at first, then many, faces calm and plain. The heavy man in the front row grips his knees, turns sharply round over his shoulder and glares at the room, eyes wide and outraged. The clerk beside him glances sideways at him, then down. The "£50" lettering stays readable on every paddle. On the right, the masked auctioneer remains completely still behind the lectern, gavel held up, balaclava with its white ring and red triangle over his left eye exactly as it is, gloved hands only. No one talks. Sound: shuffle of chairs and paddles, a swelling murmur of a crowd, soft rain on canvas. Natural daylight inside the marquee.

The man in the flat cap holds the framed picture up towards the camera, gives it a little waggle and grins. He says, cheerfully, in a rough English market-trader voice: "Hospitals, love. Forty quid." Light rain drips from the edge of the gazebo, people walk past behind him. Camera steady at chest height. The words on the small tag stay the same.

Camera holds still. The grinning trader in the flat cap lifts the picture frame a little higher for the customer and says, in a chirpy English accent: "Hospitals, love. Forty quid." Then he raises his eyebrows, waiting. Drizzle, shoppers in hoods pass in the background. Nobody else speaks.

Camera steady at chest height. The grinning man in the flat cap lifts the framed picture a little towards the camera and says, cheerfully, in a rough English market-trader voice: "Hospitals, love. Forty quid." Then he raises his eyebrows, waiting. Light drizzle, shoppers in hoods pass behind. The tag on the frame stays the same. Nobody else speaks.
